steps.eli5: Each sale brings in $8. It cost $3 to make. The remaining $5 goes toward covering your fixed costs first, then becomes actual profit.

steps.action: Divide fixed costs by profit per item
steps.eli5: Each item chips away $5 at the $500 fixed cost mountain. After 100 items: 100 × $5 = $500 – the mountain is gone! Item 101 is pure profit.
At 100 items: $800 in revenue, $800 in costs = $0 profit. Exactly break-even. Sell 101 items: $808 revenue, $803 costs, $5 profit.
The denominator (Price − Variable Cost) is called 'contribution margin.' It's how much each unit contributes to covering your fixed costs. This formula works for any business.

lessons.desc: VAT (Value Added Tax) is added on top of a price at the register – just like sales tax. But sometimes you're given the price ALREADY including VAT and need to back out the original price. That's reverse VAT.
lessons.problem: An item costs $92 including 15% VAT. What was the pre-tax price?

steps.action: The $92 includes both the price AND 15% on top
steps.eli5: If the original price is 100%, adding 15% VAT makes it 115% of the original. The $92 you see IS that 115%.

steps.action: Divide by 1.15 to find the original
steps.eli5: 92 ÷ 1.15 = 80. The pre-tax price was $80. The VAT portion was $92 − $80 = $12.

steps.math: DON'T do $92 × 0.15 = $13.80 and subtract. That gives the wrong answer.
steps.eli5: Applying 15% to the VAT-inclusive price gives the wrong tax amount. You must divide by 1.15, not multiply. The tax was 15% of the smaller number – not 15% of the bigger one.

lessons.desc: You're standing 10 meters from a tall tree. You look up at a 30° angle to see the top. How tall is the tree? Sine solves this – without climbing it, without measuring it.
lessons.problem: Angle = 30°, hypotenuse = 10. Find the opposite side.

steps.eli5: SOH is your memory hook. The 'opposite' side faces the angle, the 'hypotenuse' is the longest side (across from 90°). Sine is their ratio.
We know the angle (30°) and the hypotenuse (10m). We're solving for the opposite side – the tree's height.
A few trig values are worth memorizing: sin(30°) = 0.5, sin(45°) ≈ 0.71, sin(60°) ≈ 0.87, sin(90°) = 1.
The tree is 5 meters tall – figured out from 10 meters away by measuring the angle. That's exactly how surveyors and architects work!

lessons.desc: If sine finds the height (vertical), cosine finds the horizontal distance. Together they can describe any direction in 2D space.
lessons.problem: Angle = 60°, hypotenuse = 14. Find the adjacent side.

steps.eli5: The 'adjacent' side is the one right next to the angle (touching it, but not the hypotenuse). CAH = Cosine, Adjacent, Hypotenuse.
Angle = 60°, hypotenuse = 14. We want the adjacent side – the horizontal ground distance.
Coincidence: sin(30°) = cos(60°) = 0.5. They're mirror images – because 30° and 60° are complementary angles.
The adjacent side = 7. Horizontal distance is 7 units when hypotenuse is 14 and angle is 60°.

lessons.desc: Tangent skips the hypotenuse entirely – it directly compares height to ground distance. Great when you're standing on the ground measuring angles up to things.
lessons.problem: Angle = 45°, adjacent side = 8. Find the opposite side.

steps.eli5: No hypotenuse needed! Tangent directly compares the vertical (opposite) to the horizontal (adjacent). Great for surveying: you know your distance and measure the angle.
Angle = 45°. Ground distance (adjacent) = 8m. Building height (opposite) = unknown.
At exactly 45°, opposite = adjacent. They're equal! That's why tan(45°) = 1 – a perfect diagonal.
The building is 8 meters tall and you're 8 meters away. A 45° angle means you'd be looking at exactly a 45° diagonal. 🏢

lessons.desc: SOH-CAH-TOA is the password to trig. Burn it into your brain and right triangles become trivial – for life.
lessons.problem: Find angle θ if opposite = 5 and hypotenuse = 13.

steps.action: Identify what you have: opposite + hypotenuse = Sine
steps.eli5: Match what you know to SOH-CAH-TOA. We have opposite (5) and hypotenuse (13). That's SOH → use Sine.
Divide: 5 ÷ 13 ≈ 0.3846. This is the sine value of our mystery angle.

steps.action: Use inverse sine to find the angle
steps.eli5: sin⁻¹ (arcsin) undoes sine. On a calculator: [2nd] + [sin] + [0.3846]. Asks: 'what angle has this sine?'
The angle is about 22.6°. This is the 5-12-13 Pythagorean triple. Missing side? 12. Check: 5²+12²=25+144=169=13². ✓

lessons.concept: The Unit Circle – Angles and Coordinates
lessons.desc: The unit circle is a circle with radius 1 centered at the origin. Every angle has a point on this circle – and the x and y coordinates of that point ARE the cosine and sine of the angle. It's the map of all trig.
lessons.problem: Find sin(90°) and cos(90°) using the unit circle.

steps.action: Draw the unit circle – radius 1, center at origin
steps.eli5: Any point (x, y) on this circle is exactly 1 unit from the center. The circle has circumference 2π and is the foundation of all periodic math – waves, sound, electricity.

steps.math: 90° is straight up – the top of the circle
steps.eli5: Starting at 0° (rightmost point), rotate 90° counterclockwise. You end up at the very top of the circle: the point (0, 1).
On the unit circle: x = cos(angle), y = sin(angle). Always. At 90°: the point is (0, 1).
At 90°, you're pointing straight up: all vertical (sin = 1), no horizontal (cos = 0). Geometrically obvious – the unit circle makes trig visual instead of mysterious.

lessons.concept: Finding a Missing Angle with Inverse Trig
lessons.desc: When you KNOW the sides but need the ANGLE, you reverse the trig function. sin⁻¹ undoes sin, cos⁻¹ undoes cos, tan⁻¹ undoes tan. These are also called arcsin, arccos, arctan.
lessons.problem: A right triangle has adjacent = 5 and hypotenuse = 10. Find angle θ.

steps.math: We have adjacent and hypotenuse → use cosine (CAH)
steps.eli5: Match to SOH-CAH-TOA. Adjacent + Hypotenuse = CAH = Cosine. Set up: cos(θ) = adjacent/hypotenuse.
5 ÷ 10 = 0.5. So the cosine of our mystery angle is 0.5. Now reverse it.
What angle has a cosine of 0.5? We need arccos(0.5). This is one of our memorizable values!

steps.action: Evaluate – this is a special angle
steps.eli5: cos(60°) = 0.5 is a famous value. θ = 60°. The other angle in the triangle must be 30° (since 60 + 30 + 90 = 180). This is the 30-60-90 special triangle!

lessons.desc: When you look UP at something, the angle between horizontal and your line of sight is the angle of elevation. Looking DOWN, it's the angle of depression. Both are measured from the horizontal – and both use the same trig.
lessons.problem: You're 30 m from a building. The angle of elevation to the roof is 40°. How tall is the building?

steps.eli5: You (at ground level), the base of the building, and the roof form a right triangle. The ground is the adjacent side, the building height is the opposite, and your line of sight is the hypotenuse.
TOA: we have the adjacent (30m) and want the opposite (height). Tangent is perfect – it connects those two sides directly.
tan(40°) ≈ 0.839. This means for every 1 meter of horizontal distance, you gain 0.839 meters of height. Multiply by 30...
The building is about 25.2 meters tall. This is literally how engineers measure building heights, how pilots calculate descent angles, and how cameras auto-focus on distant objects.

lessons.desc: The 30-60-90 triangle has side ratios that never change: 1 : √3 : 2. Once you know one side, you know all three – without a calculator. It appears constantly in architecture, engineering, and game design.
lessons.problem: A 30-60-90 triangle has a hypotenuse of 10. Find the other two sides.

steps.eli5: The sides are ALWAYS in this ratio – no matter how big or small the triangle. The hypotenuse is always twice the short leg. The long leg is always short leg × √3 ≈ 1.73.
Since hypotenuse = 2 × short leg, divide by 2: 10 ÷ 2 = 5. The short leg (opposite 30°) = 5.
The long leg (opposite 60°) = 5√3 ≈ 8.66. This ratio is exact – no rounding needed if you leave it as 5√3.
25 + 75 = 100 = 10². The theorem confirms it. A 30-60-90 with hypotenuse 10 has legs of 5 and 5√3. Memorize this family – it saves significant calculator time.

lessons.desc: Cut a square diagonally and you get a 45-45-90 triangle. Both legs are equal, and the hypotenuse is always leg × √2. This triangle is everywhere: square rooms, baseball diamonds, tilted screens.
lessons.problem: A 45-45-90 triangle has legs of 6. Find the hypotenuse.

steps.action: Both legs equal – it's an isoceles right triangle
steps.eli5: In a 45-45-90 triangle, the two acute angles are equal (both 45°), so the two legs facing them are also equal. A perfectly symmetric right triangle.
a² + b² = c². Both a and b are 6: 36 + 36 = 72. So the hypotenuse squared = 72.
√72: split into √36 × √2 = 6√2. Numerically: 6 × 1.414 ≈ 8.49. This is why the ratio is leg × √2.
For ANY 45-45-90 triangle: hypotenuse = leg × √2. If you have the hypotenuse and need the leg: leg = hypotenuse ÷ √2. Tile installers use this daily.

lessons.desc: Degrees (360 in a circle) are intuitive but arbitrary. Radians are based on the actual geometry of a circle. Higher-level math – calculus, physics, engineering – almost exclusively uses radians. Time to meet them.
lessons.problem: Convert 180° to radians. Then convert π/3 radians to degrees.

steps.eli5: A semicircle (half turn) = π radians = 180°. This is the bridge between the two systems. One radian is about 57.3° – the angle where the arc length equals the radius.
Multiply degrees by (π/180). The 180s cancel: 180 × π/180 = π. So 180° = π radians. This is why you'll often see π scattered throughout physics formulas.
Multiply radians by (180/π). The π cancels: (π/3) × (180/π) = 180/3 = 60°. So π/3 radians = 60°.
Memorize just ONE thing: π = 180°. From there, divide or multiply to convert. Everything else follows.

lessons.desc: SOH-CAH-TOA only works for right triangles. The Law of Sines works for ANY triangle. It links every angle to the side directly across from it: the bigger the angle, the longer its opposite side.
lessons.problem: Triangle with angle A = 40°, angle B = 60°, and side a = 10. Find side b.

steps.eli5: Each side divided by the sine of its opposite angle gives the same ratio. It's like a universal exchange rate inside any triangle.
We know a=10 and A=40°. We want b, and we know B=60°. Set up those two fractions equal to each other.
Use a calculator or table. sin(60°) = √3/2 ≈ 0.866 is one of those special angles worth remembering.
Cross-multiply and solve: b = 10 × (0.866/0.643) ≈ 13.47. Side b is longer than side a because angle B (60°) is larger than angle A (40°). Makes geometric sense!

lessons.desc: What if you know all three sides but no angles? Or two sides and the included angle? The Law of Cosines handles these cases. It's the Pythagorean theorem upgraded to work for any triangle – not just right ones.
lessons.problem: Triangle with sides a = 7, b = 5, and angle C = 60°. Find side c.

steps.eli5: When C = 90°, cos(90°) = 0 and this becomes a² + b² = c² – exactly the Pythagorean theorem! The cosine term adjusts for non-right angles.
a=7, b=5, C=60°. cos(60°) = 0.5 – a special angle value worth memorizing.
√39 ≈ 6.24. The side opposite the 60° angle is about 6.24 units. As expected: it's shorter than side a (7) but longer than side b (5).

lessons.concept: Area of a Triangle Using Trig
lessons.desc: You know two sides of a triangle and the angle between them. No height given. You can still find the area! The trig formula connects two sides and their included angle directly to the area.
lessons.problem: Triangle with sides a = 8, b = 6, and included angle C = 30°. Find the area.

steps.eli5: This formula uses the angle between the two known sides (the 'included' angle). sin(C) secretly encodes the height of the triangle relative to the base.
a=8, b=6, C=30°. sin(30°) = 0.5 – a value worth memorizing cold.
½ × 8 × 6 = 24. Then × sin(30°) = × 0.5 = 12. Area = 12 square units.

steps.math: Height = b·sin(C) = 6 × 0.5 = 3.   Area = ½ × base × height = ½ × 8 × 3 = 12  ✓
steps.eli5: The height of the triangle from side a is b·sin(C). Plug that into the standard formula: ½ × base × height. Same answer. The trig formula is a built-in shortcut.

lessons.desc: The most important trig identity: sin²(θ) + cos²(θ) = 1. Always. For any angle. It's just the Pythagorean theorem applied to the unit circle. This identity is the master key for simplifying trig expressions.
lessons.problem: If sin(θ) = 3/5, find cos(θ) (assume θ is in the first quadrant).

steps.eli5: This is true for every angle. It comes from the unit circle: if (x,y) is a point on the circle, then x²+y²=1, and x=cos(θ), y=sin(θ). So cos²+sin²=1 always.
(3/5)² = 9/25. Plug it in. Now solve for cos²(θ).
Since θ is in the first quadrant, cosine is positive. cos(θ) = 4/5. Check: (3/5)²+(4/5)² = 9/25+16/25 = 25/25 = 1. ✓ This is the 3-4-5 triangle in trig form!

lessons.concept: Amplitude and Period of Sine Waves
lessons.desc: Sine waves repeat. Two key measurements tell you everything about the wave's shape: amplitude (how tall) and period (how long before it repeats). These control everything from sound pitch to AC voltage.
lessons.problem: For y = 3sin(2x), find the amplitude and period.

steps.eli5: A stretches the wave vertically (amplitude). B squishes or stretches the wave horizontally. The period is how far along x you must go before the wave repeats.
y = 3sin(2x). The 3 in front = A. The 2 inside with x = B.
The wave reaches 3 above the midline and 3 below. It swings from −3 to +3. Compare: y = sin(x) swings from −1 to +1. Tripling A triples the height.
The wave repeats every π units (about 3.14). Standard sin(x) repeats every 2π. By doubling B, we halved the period – the wave cycles twice as fast.

lessons.desc: Navigators measure direction using bearings: angles measured clockwise from due North. A ship sailing on a bearing of 060° is heading northeast. Trig turns bearing problems into right triangle calculations.
lessons.problem: A ship travels 40 km on a bearing of 030°. How far North and how far East has it gone?

steps.math: Hypotenuse = 40 km (distance traveled).  Angle from North = 30°.
steps.eli5: The ship's path is the hypotenuse. North is the vertical axis. East is horizontal. The angle between North and the ship's direction is 30°.
The northward component is the side adjacent to the 30° angle. CAH: cos(30°) = adjacent/hypotenuse → adjacent = 40 × cos(30°).
The eastward component is opposite the 30° angle. SOH: sin(30°) = opposite/hypotenuse → opposite = 40 × sin(30°) = 20 km.
34.64² ≈ 1200. 20² = 400. 1200 + 400 = 1600 = 40². ✓ GPS and maritime navigation use exactly this kind of vector decomposition.

lessons.desc: A phase shift slides a sine or cosine wave left or right without changing its shape. In y = sin(x − c), the minus c pushes the whole wave c units to the RIGHT. It's the difference between noon and 3pm on a daily temperature cycle.
lessons.problem: For y = sin(x − π/2), find the phase shift and describe what it looks like.

steps.math: Phase shift = c (positive c → shift right)
steps.eli5: The minus sign inside means a rightward shift. If it's y = sin(x + c), the plus shifts LEFT. Counterintuitive? Remember: minus pushes the wave forward (right).

steps.math: c = π/2 → wave shifts right by π/2 units
steps.eli5: The entire sine wave slides π/2 units to the right. Every feature (peaks, valleys, crossings) moves π/2 units rightward.
This is a famous identity. Shifting sine right by π/2 gives you a flipped cosine. Sine and cosine are the same wave – just offset by 90°. They're the same song, different starting point.

steps.action: What changes, what stays the same
steps.math: Amplitude = 1 (unchanged).  Period = 2π (unchanged).  Shape identical – just moved.
steps.eli5: Phase shift only moves the wave; it doesn't stretch or compress it. Amplitude and period stay exactly the same.

lessons.desc: sin(2θ) is not 2·sin(θ). Trig doesn't scale like that. The double angle formula is a specific identity that links the trig of 2θ back to the trig of θ. It appears constantly in calculus and physics.
lessons.problem: If sin(θ) = 4/5 and θ is in the first quadrant, find sin(2θ).

steps.action: The double angle formula for sine
steps.eli5: This is exact – not an approximation. sin(2θ) = 2·sin(θ)·cos(θ) always. Memorize it.

steps.action: Find cos(θ) using the Pythagorean identity
steps.eli5: We know sin(θ) = 4/5. From the identity: cos²(θ) = 1 − 16/25 = 9/25. Since θ is in Q1, cos is positive: cos(θ) = 3/5.

steps.math: sin(2θ) = 24/25 = 0.96, which is close to 1 (makes sense for a large angle)
steps.eli5: If sin(θ) = 4/5, then θ ≈ 53°. So 2θ ≈ 106°. sin(106°) ≈ 0.96. ✓ The formula gives the right answer.

lessons.desc: Solve sin(x) = 0.5. You know sin(30°) = 0.5, so x = 30°. But wait – sine is also 0.5 at 150°. And again at 390°, 510°... Trig equations have infinite solutions. Knowing where to look for them all is the skill.
lessons.problem: Solve sin(x) = 0.5 for 0° ≤ x < 360°.

steps.action: Find the principal solution using inverse sine
steps.eli5: The calculator gives you one answer: 30°. But there may be more within the given range. Always check!

steps.action: Use the sine symmetry: sin is also positive in Quadrant II
steps.eli5: Sine is positive in Quadrants I and II (above the x-axis on the unit circle). The QII solution mirrors the QI solution across the y-axis: 180° − 30° = 150°.
sin(150°) = 0.5. Confirmed.

steps.math: QI: 30°.  QII: 150°.  QIII & QIV: sine is negative → no more solutions.
steps.eli5: sin is negative in Q3 and Q4. Since we need 0.5 (positive), only Q1 and Q2 yield solutions. Final answers: x = 30° and x = 150°.

lessons.desc: A handful of trig values come up so often that professionals have them memorized. 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°. These are the special angles – knowing them cold lets you solve problems without a calculator.
lessons.problem: Without a calculator, find: sin(45°), cos(30°), and tan(60°).

steps.eli5: A 45-45-90 triangle has legs 1 and 1, hypotenuse √2. sin(45°) = opposite/hyp = 1/√2 = √2/2. The equal legs make this triangle perfectly symmetric.
A 30-60-90 triangle has sides 1, √3, 2. cos(30°) = adjacent/hypotenuse = √3/2. The side adjacent to the 30° angle is √3, hypotenuse is 2.
tan(60°) = opposite/adjacent = √3/1 = √3. At 60°, the opposite side (√3) is longer than the adjacent side (1). Makes sense for a steep angle!

steps.math: sin: 30°=½, 45°=√2/2, 60°=√3/2.   cos: same values in reverse!
steps.eli5: Cos values for 30°, 45°, 60° are exactly the sin values in reverse order. This isn't a coincidence – sin(θ) = cos(90°−θ). Complementary angles swap sine and cosine.

lessons.desc: A prime number only has two factors: 1 and itself. It refuses to break into equal groups. Primes are math's fundamental loners – and every other number is secretly built from them.
lessons.problem: Is 37 a prime number?

steps.action: Smart shortcut: only check up to √37
steps.eli5: If 37 had a factor bigger than 6, it would also have one smaller (they come in pairs). So we only need to check divisors up to √37 ≈ 6. Just three checks.
Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8. 37 ends in 7 – it's odd. Eliminated instantly.
Divisibility trick for 3: add the digits. 3+7=10. Is 10 divisible by 3? No. So 3 doesn't divide into 37.

steps.math: 37 ends in 7, not 0 or 5 → NO  →  37 is prime! 🎉
steps.eli5: Numbers divisible by 5 always end in 0 or 5. 37 ends in 7. Nope! We've checked all candidates up to √37. 37 is PRIME.

lessons.desc: You have 24 apples and 36 oranges. You want to make identical gift bags – same number of each, nothing left over. The GCF tells you the maximum number of bags you can make.
lessons.problem: Find the GCF of 24 and 36.

steps.eli5: Factors divide in without a remainder. For 24: try 1 (1×24), 2 (2×12), 3 (3×8), 4 (4×6). You get: 1,2,3,4,6,8,12,24.
These numbers appear in BOTH lists. Any of these would let you split both groups equally.
GCF = 12. You can make 12 bags with 2 apples and 3 oranges each. 12 × 2 = 24 apples, 12 × 3 = 36 oranges. Nothing left over. 🎁

lessons.desc: Bus A comes every 4 minutes. Bus B comes every 6 minutes. Both just arrived together. When's the next time they arrive at the same time? The LCM tells you.
lessons.problem: Find the LCM of 4 and 6.

steps.eli5: Multiples of 4 = skip-counting by 4. Bus A arrives at minutes: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20…
Skip-count by 6. Bus B arrives at minutes: 6, 12, 18, 24…
Minute 12 appears on BOTH lists! LCM = 12. If you just missed them, you wait 12 minutes. 🚌🚌

lessons.desc: Even and odd numbers follow strict rules when you add or multiply them. Once you know the rules, you can predict results without doing any arithmetic.
lessons.problem: Without calculating, is (27 × 34 + 15) even or odd?

steps.action: 27 is odd, 34 is even – what's odd × even?
steps.eli5: Rules: odd×odd=odd, even×even=even, odd×even=EVEN. Any even number has a factor of 2. Multiply anything by an even number → always a multiple of 2 = even.
More rules: even+even=even, odd+odd=even, even+odd=ODD. Add one extra (odd) and there's always one left hanging.
We figured that out without a calculator. These parity rules work for any numbers, any size. That's number theory magic!

lessons.desc: Divisibility rules let you check if a number is divisible by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, or 10 without doing any division. These are tricks mathematicians discovered by studying number patterns.
lessons.problem: Is 732 divisible by 2? By 3? By 9?

steps.action: Divisible by 2? Check if it's even
steps.eli5: Rule for 2: last digit is 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8. 732 ends in 2. Divisible by 2. Simple as checking one digit.
Rule for 3: add ALL the digits. If the sum is divisible by 3, so is the whole number. 7+3+2=12, and 12÷3=4. So 732 is divisible by 3.

steps.action: Divisible by 9? Sum the digits again
steps.eli5: Rule for 9: same as 3, but the digit sum must be divisible by 9. 12 ÷ 9 = 1 remainder 3. Not divisible by 9.
Rule for 6: divisible by BOTH 2 AND 3. 732 passes both tests, so it's divisible by 6. You can verify: 732 ÷ 6 = 122. ✓

lessons.desc: Every whole number greater than 1 is either prime, or can be built by multiplying primes together. 12 = 2 × 2 × 3. This 'prime recipe' is always unique – like a fingerprint. It's the foundation of GCF, LCM, and cryptography.
lessons.problem: Find the prime factorization of 60.

steps.action: Divide by the smallest prime that fits
steps.eli5: Start with 2 – the smallest prime. Does 2 divide into 60? Yes (60 is even). 60 = 2 × 30. Now do the same to 30.
30 is even: 30 = 2 × 15. Now 15: not even, try 3. 1+5=6, divisible by 3! 15 = 3 × 5. And 5 is prime – we stop.
The full recipe for 60: two 2s, one 3, one 5. Written cleanly: 2² × 3 × 5. Every time you break 60 down this way, you get the exact same answer.
4 × 15 = 60. Confirmed! The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says this prime fingerprint is unique – no other combination of primes multiplies to 60.

lessons.desc: The Euclidean Algorithm is a 2,300-year-old method to find the GCF of two large numbers – without factoring them. It's one of the oldest algorithms still in active use (including in encryption today).
lessons.problem: Find the GCF of 48 and 18 using the Euclidean Algorithm.

steps.action: Divide the larger number by the smaller
steps.eli5: 48 = 18 × 2 + 12. The remainder is 12. The key insight: GCF(48, 18) = GCF(18, 12). The GCF doesn't change when you replace the bigger number with the remainder.
18 = 12 × 1 + 6. Remainder is 6. So GCF(18, 12) = GCF(12, 6).
12 = 6 × 2 + 0. Remainder is 0. When the remainder hits 0, we're done!

steps.action: The GCF is the last non-zero remainder
steps.eli5: The last non-zero remainder = 6. So GCF(48, 18) = 6. This algorithm handles huge numbers (think 10-digit) in just a few steps – it's why it's still used in cryptography.

lessons.desc: A perfect number equals the sum of all its proper factors (divisors except itself). 6 = 1 + 2 + 3. Perfect numbers are vanishingly rare – only a handful are known – and they've fascinated mathematicians for 2,500 years.
lessons.problem: Show that 28 is a perfect number.

steps.eli5: Proper factors = all divisors except the number itself. For 28: 1×28, 2×14, 4×7. Proper factors: 1, 2, 4, 7, 14.
1+2=3, +4=7, +7=14, +14=28. The sum equals 28 exactly. 28 is a perfect number!

steps.action: The known perfect numbers are rare
steps.eli5: There are only a few known perfect numbers – all of them even. No odd perfect number has ever been found, and no one has proven they don't exist. One of math's oldest open questions!
Every even perfect number is tied to a Mersenne prime (a prime of the form 2ⁿ−1). 2³−1 = 7 is prime, so 2²×7 = 28 is perfect. The hunt for large perfect numbers IS the hunt for large primes.

lessons.desc: On a 12-hour clock, 10 o'clock + 5 hours = 3 o'clock, not 15. That's modular arithmetic – where numbers wrap around after hitting a limit. It powers everything from encryption to checksums to day-of-week calculations.
lessons.problem: Today is Wednesday. What day is it 100 days from now?

steps.math: Mon=1, Tue=2, Wed=3, Thu=4, Fri=5, Sat=6, Sun=0
steps.eli5: We'll use 0–6 for the 7 days (mod 7). Wednesday = 3. We want to figure out 3 + 100, then wrap around.

steps.action: Divide 100 by 7 and find the remainder
steps.eli5: 14 complete weeks = 98 days (exact same day of the week). The leftover 2 days are what actually move us forward. 100 mod 7 = 2.

steps.action: Add the remainder to the starting day
steps.eli5: Wednesday (3) + 2 days forward = Friday (5). So 100 days from Wednesday is a Friday!

steps.action: Real world: this is how calendars work
steps.math: The '100 mod 7' step is the key – only remainders matter
steps.eli5: Same logic tells you: born on a Tuesday? Birthday in 365 days = Tuesday (365 mod 7 = 1, so +1 day: Wednesday). This math drives scheduling software, crypto, and barcode checksums.

lessons.desc: Start with 0 and 1. Each new number is the sum of the two before it. Simple rule, endlessly surprising consequences – Fibonacci numbers appear in flower petals, shell spirals, stock markets, and computer algorithms.
lessons.problem: List the first 10 Fibonacci numbers and find the 10th.

steps.action: The rule: each number = sum of the two before it
steps.eli5: Starting seeds: 0, 1. Then: 0+1=1, 1+1=2, 1+2=3, 2+3=5, 3+5=8, 5+8=13, 8+13=21, 13+21=34. Each term adds the previous two.

steps.action: Consecutive ratios approach the Golden Ratio
steps.eli5: Divide any Fibonacci number by the previous one: 34/21 ≈ 1.619. As you go further, this ratio approaches φ (phi) = 1.618… – the famous Golden Ratio found in art, architecture, and nature.

steps.action: Where Fibonacci numbers appear in nature
steps.math: Sunflower seeds: 34 spirals one way, 55 the other – both Fibonacci!
steps.eli5: Flower petals come in Fibonacci counts (3, 5, 8, 13…). Pinecone scales: Fibonacci spirals. Nautilus shells: Fibonacci proportions. The sequence emerges wherever nature packs things efficiently.

lessons.desc: Two numbers are coprime (also called relatively prime) if the only number that divides both of them is 1. They don't need to be prime themselves – just share no common factors. This concept is the backbone of fraction simplification and encryption.
lessons.problem: Are 14 and 15 coprime?

steps.eli5: 14 breaks down into 2 and 7. Both prime.
15 breaks down into 3 and 5. Both prime.

steps.action: Do they share any prime factors?
steps.eli5: Compare the prime ingredient lists. 14 uses {2, 7}. 15 uses {3, 5}. No shared factors. GCF = 1.

14 and 15 are consecutive integers – consecutive integers are ALWAYS coprime because a common factor > 1 can't divide two numbers that differ by exactly 1. Fractions with consecutive denominators are always fully reduced from the start.

lessons.desc: Square numbers are what you get when you multiply an integer by itself: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25... They form an unbroken pattern with a surprising trick: the difference between consecutive squares is always the next odd number.
lessons.problem: What are the first 8 square numbers? What's the pattern in their differences?

steps.eli5: Square each integer: 1×1=1, 2×2=4, 3×3=9, and so on. Geometrically, these are the areas of squares with side lengths 1, 2, 3...

steps.action: Find the differences between consecutive squares
steps.eli5: The gaps are 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15 – consecutive odd numbers! Every time you go to the next square, the jump is the next odd number.
The difference between the nth and (n+1)th square is always 2n+1. For n=1: 3. n=2: 5. n=3: 7. That's exactly the odd numbers.

steps.action: Use this to find the next square quickly
steps.eli5: Instead of computing 9² = 81, just add the next odd number: 64 + 17 = 81. This pattern lets you generate squares rapidly without multiplying.

lessons.desc: Arrange bowling pins in a triangle: 1 pin, then 2, then 3 – totaling 6 pins. Triangular numbers count how many objects fill an equilateral triangle. They appear in handshakes, staircase steps, and combinations.
lessons.problem: Find the 8th triangular number.

steps.action: Triangular numbers: sum of first n integers
steps.eli5: The nth triangular number = total objects in a triangle with n rows. Row 1: 1 dot. Row 2: 2 dots. Total = 1+2+...+n.
Gauss's trick: pair 1 with n, 2 with n−1, etc. Each pair sums to n+1. There are n/2 pairs. So total = n(n+1)/2. Young Gauss used this to sum 1–100 in seconds at age 7.
8 × 9 = 72. 72 ÷ 2 = 36. The 8th triangular number is 36.

steps.action: Fun connection: square numbers = sum of two triangular numbers
steps.eli5: Every square number is the sum of two consecutive triangular numbers. 28 + 36 = 64 = 8². These number families are all connected in beautiful ways.

lessons.concept: GCF and LCM via Prime Factorization
lessons.desc: The prime factorization method for GCF and LCM works perfectly for any numbers, even large ones. GCF takes the MINIMUM of each prime's power. LCM takes the MAXIMUM. Two rules, same prime factorizations.
lessons.problem: Find GCF and LCM of 36 and 60 using prime factorization.

steps.action: GCF: take the MINIMUM power of each shared prime
steps.eli5: Both have 2²: take 2². 36 has 3², 60 has 3¹: take the smaller, 3¹. 5 is only in 60 – doesn't appear in GCF. GCF = 4 × 3 = 12.

steps.action: LCM: take the MAXIMUM power of each prime
steps.eli5: Take the highest power of each prime that appears in EITHER factorization. 2²: same in both → 4. 3²: 36 wins → 9. 5¹: only in 60 → 5. LCM = 4 × 9 × 5 = 180.

steps.action: Golden relationship: GCF × LCM = product of the two numbers
steps.eli5: Always true: GCF(a,b) × LCM(a,b) = a × b. This is a great quick check and a useful identity.

lessons.desc: Our normal system uses base 10 (digits 0–9). Computers use base 2 (digits 0 and 1 only). Every number can be represented in binary. Understanding binary unlocks computers, data storage, and logic gates.
lessons.problem: Convert 19 to binary. Then convert 10110 (binary) to decimal.

steps.action: Decimal to binary: divide by 2, collect remainders
steps.eli5: Divide repeatedly by 2. Track the remainders. Read them BOTTOM to TOP: 1, 0, 0, 1, 1. So 19 = 10011 in binary.
Each position is a power of 2. Rightmost = 2⁰=1, then 2¹=2, 2²=4, 2³=8, 2⁴=16. Add the powers where you see a 1: 16+2+1=19.
Positions with a 1: the 2⁴=16 spot, the 2²=4 spot, and the 2¹=2 spot. Sum: 16+4+2 = 22.

lessons.desc: Casting out nines is a quick arithmetic check technique: the digit sum of a number has the same remainder when divided by 9 as the number itself. Use it to spot errors in multiplication without doing the full calculation again.
lessons.problem: Quickly verify: 57 × 83 = 4,731 using casting out nines.

steps.eli5: Add the digits of 57: 5+7=12. 12 isn't a single digit, so add again: 1+2=3. The digital root of 57 is 3.
Digital root of 83: 8+3=11 → 1+1=2.
The digital root of the product should equal the digital root of (3 × 2) = 6.

steps.action: Find digital root of 4,731 and compare
steps.eli5: Digital root of 4,731 is 6. Matches! This doesn't prove the answer is right (it could be a lucky coincidence), but if the digital roots DON'T match, the answer is definitely wrong. Great error-catching tool.

lessons.answer: Digital roots match (6 = 6) → calculation checks out

lessons.desc: When you divide integers, the result isn't always clean. The Division Algorithm formally states: for any integers a and b (b > 0), there exist unique integers q (quotient) and r (remainder) such that a = bq + r and 0 ≤ r < b.
lessons.problem: Express 47 ÷ 5 in the form a = bq + r.

steps.eli5: 5 goes into 47 nine full times (5 × 9 = 45). 47 − 45 = 2 left over. Quotient q = 9, remainder r = 2.

steps.action: Write in the formal form a = bq + r
steps.eli5: Check: 5 × 9 = 45. 45 + 2 = 47. ✓ This is the Division Algorithm statement.
The remainder must be non-negative AND less than the divisor. 2 is between 0 and 4 (inclusive). If r were ≥ 5, you could have divided once more – the quotient would be wrong.

steps.math: Uniqueness: there's exactly one valid q and r for any a and b.
steps.eli5: This might seem obvious, but the formal guarantee – exactly one quotient and remainder – is the foundation for number theory proofs, the Euclidean algorithm, and modular arithmetic.

lessons.desc: A palindromic number reads the same forwards and backwards: 121, 1331, 99, 7. They're a fun number theory topic with surprising patterns. The 'reverse and add' algorithm can turn most numbers into palindromes in just a few steps.
lessons.problem: Is 143 a palindrome? If not, apply reverse-and-add until you get one.

steps.action: Check: does 143 read the same backwards?
steps.eli5: Flip the digits: 1-4-3 becomes 3-4-1. 341 ≠ 143, so 143 is not a palindrome.
Reverse 143 to get 341, then add them together. 143 + 341 = 484.
4-8-4 backwards is still 4-8-4. 484 is a palindrome! One step was enough for 143.
Powers of repunit numbers (all 1s) always produce palindromes! 11² = 121, 111² = 12321, 1111² = 1234321. The pattern climbs to the middle and comes back down symmetrically.

lessons.desc: The Sieve of Eratosthenes is a 2,200-year-old algorithm for finding ALL prime numbers up to a limit. You start by crossing off multiples of 2, then 3, then 5 – whatever's left uncrossed is prime. Simple and still used in modern computing.
lessons.problem: Find all primes up to 30 using the Sieve.

steps.eli5: Start with every candidate. We'll eliminate composites until only primes remain. We start at 2 – the smallest prime.

steps.action: Cross off all multiples of 2 (except 2 itself)
steps.eli5: Every even number > 2 is divisible by 2, so it's composite. One sweep eliminates half the candidates.

steps.action: Cross off multiples of 3, then 5 (next uncrossed numbers)
steps.eli5: 6,12,18... were already gone. New eliminations from 3: 9,15,21,27. From 5: only 25 is new. 7's multiples (49...) are all past 30.

steps.action: The survivors are the primes up to 30
steps.eli5: Ten primes below 30. The Sieve is optimal for finding all primes up to a limit – much faster than testing each number individually. Modern prime-finding algorithms are souped-up versions of this ancient method.

lessons.desc: In 1742, Christian Goldbach wrote to Euler with a simple claim: every even number greater than 2 can be written as the sum of two primes. 4=2+2, 6=3+3, 8=3+5, 100=3+97. Simple to state, never proven. One of math's oldest unsolved problems.
lessons.problem: Express 28, 50, and 100 as the sum of two primes.

steps.eli5: 5 and 23 are both prime: 5+23=28. ✓ There can be multiple ways. 11+17=28 also works. Goldbach doesn't require uniqueness – just that at least one way exists.
Three different ways for 50. The bigger the number, generally the more pairs there are. This trend is one reason mathematicians believe the conjecture is true – it gets 'easier,' not harder.
Four ways for 100. The conjecture has been verified by computer for all even numbers up to 4 × 10¹⁸ (4 quintillion). Still not proven for all numbers.

steps.math: Primes are distributed irregularly – no formula predicts them. That irregularity makes proofs about their sums extremely hard.
steps.eli5: We can CHECK any specific number. But proving it works for EVERY even number forever – infinite cases – requires a deep theorem nobody has found yet. This is what makes pure math beautiful and humbling.
